prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Othello (Reversi) on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you: np.ndarray, opponent: np.ndarray) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move when `policy` is called. - `you` and `opponent` are 8x8 numpy arrays containing only 0/1 integers. - `you[r][c] == 1` means your disc is at row `r`, col `c`. - `opponent[r][c] == 1` means the opponent disc is at row `r`, col `c`. - An empty cell means `you[r][c] == 0` and `opponent[r][c] == 0`. - Positions are valid: never `you[r][c] == opponent[r][c] == 1`. - Move coordinates use algebraic notation: columns `a..h` map to `c = 0..7`, rows `1..8` map to `r = 0..7`. For example, `a4` maps to you[3][0] - The game ends when neither player has a legal move (or the board is full). - Objective: finish with more discs than the opponent; ties are draws. # Action / Return Format - Return a move string like `"d3"` (file letter `a..h` + rank `1..8`). - A legal move must place a disc on an empty cell that flips at least one opponent disc in any direction. - Flips occur along any of the 8 directions where the new disc brackets a contiguous line of opponent discs ending in your disc. - If you have no legal moves, return `"pass"`. You may not return `"pass"` if you have legal moves. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm designing an Othello AI using bitboards for efficient board representation and move generation, then layering in alpha-beta search with iterative deepening to explore the game tree strategically. The evaluation function will weight positional factors like corners and edges heavily while considering mobility, and I'll add an endgame solver to play perfectly when the board is nearly full.

Writing the bitboard implementation... Writing the move generation function... Defining shift helper functions...

Now I'm setting up the move generation logic—finding all valid moves by checking each direction from the player's pieces, sliding through opponent discs until hitting an empty square or the player's own piece, then marking those landing spots as valid moves.

For making a move, I'm tracing through each direction from the chosen square to identify which opponent discs get flipped, then updating the board state accordingly.

I'm incorporating position weights for standard Othello strategy—corners are valuable, edges are risky, and the center squares are neutral—then combining that with mobility scoring and corner control to evaluate board positions.

Setting up alpha-beta pruning with iterative deepening and a one-second time limit, searching 4-6 moves deep in the midgame and solving the endgame completely when there are 10-12 or fewer empty squares remaining.

Now I'm implementing the core engine with bit manipulation for efficiency, using popcount to track disc counts and compiling all the shift operations for the eight directions.

Implementing the move generation and board update logic...

Setting up position evaluation with a weight matrix for strategic positioning, then calculating mobility as a factor in the score. The current approach iterates through all 64 squares which is slow, so I'm thinking about precomputing weight masks or using popcount with bitmasks to speed this up.

Now I'm mapping out the weight groups by their values across the board—corners at 100, X-squares at -50, edge positions at various weights, and the center squares at 1—then identifying which bit positions correspond to each group so I can create efficient bitmasks for evaluation.

I'll compute these masks programmatically by iterating through all 64 squares, grouping them by their weight value, and building a dictionary that maps each weight to its corresponding bitmask. Then during position evaluation, I can quickly calculate the score by iterating through each weight group, using bit_count to count player and opponent pieces in that group, and multiplying by the weight.

For the search algorithm, I'm implementing alpha-beta pruning with a time deadline check, starting with move ordering that prioritizes corners, then handling terminal states where either both players pass or the game ends. Writing the policy function...

I'm realizing the alphabeta function needs to handle timeouts more gracefully—using an exception-based approach makes it cleaner to break out of the iterative deepening loop when time runs out, so I only use fully completed search results. I'm also thinking about move ordering and evaluation efficiency, particularly whether mobility calculations are worth the cost during leaf node evaluation.

Implementing the core search with bitwise operations... Defining the game logic functions... Writing the move conversion and policy logic...

Now I'm setting up the main policy function that converts board arrays to bitboards, then uses iterative deepening to search for the best move within the time limit. For endgames with few pieces remaining, I'm doing a full solve, otherwise I'm progressively deepening the search until time runs out. There's a concern about the endgame depth parameter that I need to think through.

The issue is that when passes occur, they shouldn't count as depth consumed, but my current setup decrements depth on each recursive call regardless. For endgame solving, I want to search until the game actually ends, so I should set the depth high enough to cover all remaining moves plus passes. Since passes don't consume empty squares, setting depth equal to the number of empties should be sufficient to reach terminal positions, and the base case of both players having no moves will catch the end of game.

For performance, I'm estimating that with alpha-beta pruning and good move ordering, I can explore around 10,000-20,000 nodes within a 1-second budget, which should handle depth 4-5 searches in the midgame. I'll also optimize the bit-counting operations using Python's built-in methods to speed up position evaluation.

Setting up helper functions... Setting up the core bitboard utilities...

Now I'm implementing the move generation logic that finds all valid moves by checking in each direction for opponent pieces followed by empty squares, then building the make_move function to flip captured pieces along valid lines. After that comes the evaluation functions—one that scores positions based on piece weights and mobility, another for endgame final scores—and finally the alphabeta search that recursively explores the game tree with alpha-beta pruning and timeout handling.

Finishing the utility functions... Implementing the move logic...

The make_move function traces in each direction from the placed disc, collecting opponent pieces until hitting either an empty square or one of our own pieces—if we find our piece, we flip all the collected opponent pieces in that direction. The shift functions handle board boundaries automatically by returning zero at edges, so the loop naturally terminates. I'm also verifying that the alphabeta search correctly handles pass moves by returning None and checking before updating the best move, and that the negamax scoring properly inverts perspective when roles flip. The terminal condition catches endgame states even if the search goes deep early on. This should be solid.
